html:
Henry Morton Stanley was a Welsh-born journalist and explorer who crossed Central Africa and then helped King Leopold II of Belgium claim the Congo. He was born John Rowlands in 1841, grew up partly in a workhouse, and went to America as a young man, where he took a new name and fought on both sides of the American Civil War.

As a reporter for the New York Herald, he was sent to find the missionary David Livingstone, who had not been heard from for years. He found him at Ujiji on Lake Tanganyika in 1871 and, by his own account, greeted him with "Dr. Livingstone, I presume?"

From 1874 to 1877 he crossed Africa from Zanzibar to the Atlantic and traced the Congo river to the sea. For part of the way he travelled with the Swahili-Arab trader Tippu Tip, with help from rulers such as the lord of Utetera. He fought his way down the river, and more than half of his party died.

From 1879 he worked for Leopold, building a road and stations along the lower Congo and making chiefs sign treaties. In 1881 he founded Leopoldville, today's Kinshasa, on land of the Teke. This work laid the base of the Congo Free State and its brutal rubber regime. Africans called him Bula Matari, "breaker of rocks". He later led a costly expedition to relieve Emin Pasha in Sudan, was knighted and sat in the British Parliament.
